To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the NII domain fragment is not a good model for intact transferrins, that the fragment binds iron via the synergistic carbonate and two tyrosine ligands, but that the binding is not as strong as in the intact proteins, and that the iron is bound in a similar manner by both the fragment and the intact proteins.

The 18 kDa protein fragment of duck ovoferrin, corresponding in sequence and function to the NII-domain of the intact protein and lacking the two aspartate and the single histidine residues involved in iron binding, binds iron in an analogous manner to intact ovoferrin.

the 18 kDA fragment of ovotransferring binds iron in a manner almost indistinguishable from the intact protein, but the aspartate/histidine ligand has been replaced by glycine or nitrilotriacetic acid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure of the 18kDa NII domain of duck ovotranferrin and the mechanism of its iron binding.
the mechanism of iron uptake and release from transferrins, and the structure-function relationship of the transferrins and their analogues, in particular the role of the synergistic carbonate.
the structure and function of proteins and nucleic acids, and in particular, with the mechanism of action of metalloproteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
iron is bound in the 18 kda fragment of duck ovtransferrin by a synergistic carbonate anionic complex with one tyrosine and the amino and carboxy termini of a glycine peptide.
iron binding by the 18 kDA fragment of duck ovoferritin is not the same as in the intact protein and that the fragment is not an appropriate model for the intact protein.
iron binding to the 18kDa NII fragment of ovotransferring is a mixture of glycine and peptides from the preparation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 18 kda fragment of duck ovtransferrin is not a simple NII domain.
iron binding by transferrin is not a simple process and that the binding sites in the NII domains of ovotransferring and lactoferrin are not identical.
the NII domain fragment is not an appropriate model for iron binding by the intact protein and, in the case of duck ovotrnsferrin, the NII domain is probably not a functional iron-binding site.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the iron is bound to the 18kDa fragment of duck Ovotransferrins by two tyrosine, a carbonate anion, a nitrilotriacetic acid and a peptide.
the iron binding site in the 18 kD NII domain is not the same as that in intact ovotransferring.
the 18 kda fragment is an important part of the iron binding site of transferrins.
